html:
The Parintintin are a Kawahib people of the lower Madeira River in Amazonas state, Brazil, near the town of Humaitá. They speak a language of the Tupi-Guarani branch of the Tupian family, shared with other Kawahib groups such as the Tenharim and Jupaú.

In the late 1800s, during the rubber boom, they were feared by rubber tappers for fierce attacks on anyone who came into their forests. In the early 1920s agents of Brazil's Indian Protection Service, including the ethnologist Curt Nimuendajú, made peaceful contact. Disease then cut their numbers sharply, and only a few hundred Parintintin live today.
